note: From 'heten' (to be called), cognate with the old English 'hight'. Formal: 'Hoe heet u?'. The answer is 'Ik heet ...'.

example.target: Hoe heet je? Ik heet Lisa.
example.en: What is your name? My name is Lisa.

note: Informal 'hi' among friends, family and colleagues. The 'oi' sounds like English 'oy'. Also used when leaving.
Written as one word. 'Goed' is cognate with English 'good'; the 'g' is the famous Dutch throat sound, softer in Flanders. Used until about noon.

example.en: Good morning, did you sleep well?

note: 'Middag' means afternoon (roughly 12 to 6), not just midday. Common in shops and on the phone.
Note the extra -n- (goedenavond) because 'avond' starts with a vowel. Said on arrival in the evening, not when leaving.
From 'wel te rusten' (well to rest). The normal thing to say before bed; 'goedenacht' is also used but sounds more formal.

example.en: Good night and see you tomorrow!

note: Short for 'goedendag'. Works both as a greeting and, more often, as a friendly goodbye. Cognate with English 'day'.
The usual way to introduce yourself; 'mijn naam is ...' is more formal. 'Heet' is also the adjective 'hot', so 'ik ben heet' is a classic learner mistake.
Very informal and very Dutch, often doubled: 'doei doei!'. Also 'doeg'. Not used in Flanders, where people say 'salu' or 'dag'.
For later the same day. 'Tot zo' is even sooner (in a moment); 'tot later' is vaguer.
'Geen' is the negative article ('no, not any'). A common reply to thanks or apologies, alongside 'geeft niet' (it doesn't matter).
'U' is the polite form of 'you', like French 'vous'. Also written 'dankuwel'. In Flanders 'u' is used more widely than in the Netherlands.
The past participle of 'bedanken' (to thank), used as a quick 'thanks'. 'Hartelijk bedankt' = thanks a lot.
'Fijn' (fine, nice) + 'dag'. Shop staff say 'fijne dag nog!' (still a nice day). Same pattern: 'fijn weekend', 'fijne vakantie', 'fijne avond'.
Formal twin of 'alsjeblieft', with polite 'u'. Often abbreviated 'a.u.b.' on signs. Shop staff say it when giving you your change.
'Graag' means gladly and is one of the most useful Dutch words: 'ik wil graag' = I would like. 'Geen dank' is another reply.
Borrowed from English and used constantly, for small apologies and to get attention. 'Het spijt me' is the fuller 'I'm sorry'.
From French. Used to squeeze past someone, to ask someone to repeat, or for 'excuse me?'. Stress on the second syllable.
Literally 'how goes it?', with 'het' (it) as subject. Fuller: 'Hoe gaat het met je?' (informal) or 'met u?' (formal).
The stock reply to 'hoe gaat het?'. 'Jou' is the stressed object form of 'je'. Formal version: 'Goed, en met u?'
Pronounced 'yah'; Dutch 'j' is always English 'y'. 'Ja hoor' is a relaxed 'yes, sure'; 'jawel' contradicts a negative question.
Long 'ay' sound, like English 'nay'. 'Nee hoor' softens it to a friendly 'no, not at all'. Flemish often says 'neen' in writing.
Said while shaking hands when introduced; short for 'aangenaam kennis te maken' (pleasant to make acquaintance). Slightly formal.
Cognate with English 'welcome' ('wel' + 'komen', to come). 'Welkom in Nederland!'
Like German 'Gesundheit'. 'Gezond' = healthy, '-heid' = -ness/-hood. Also used as a toast: 'op je gezondheid'.
From Latin 'nullus'. In phone numbers and scores you say 'nul'; 'nul komma vijf' = 0.5 (Dutch uses a decimal comma).
The accents distinguish the number from the article 'een' (a, an), which is pronounced with a weak 'uh'. Dropped where no confusion is possible.
Cognate with English 'two' (the w is still pronounced). 'Twee' plus 'tig' gives 'twintig', twenty.
Cognate with 'three'; where English has 'th', Dutch usually has 'd' (drie/three, dank/thank, denken/think).
Pronounced 'veer'. Dutch 'v' at the start of a word often sounds close to an English 'f', especially in the north.
Contains the 'ij' sound, often counted as a single letter in Dutch and capitalised as IJ (IJsselmeer). Roughly 'vayf'.
Cognate with 'six'. The Dutch 'z' is a real voiced z, unlike German 'sechs'.
Cognate with 'seven'. In some bakeries and offices 'zeven' is pronounced 'zeuven' to avoid confusion with 'negen' on the phone.
The 'ch' is the same rough throat sound as Dutch 'g'. Cognate with 'eight' and German 'acht'.
Cognate with 'nine'. The two 'g' sounds are both throaty; the final -en is a weak 'uh' and the n often disappears in speech.
Pronounced 'teen'. Cognate with English 'ten'; '-tien' forms thirteen to nineteen (dertien, veertien, vijftien...).
Same spelling as English 'elf' (the creature is also 'elf' in Dutch). Cognate with 'eleven'.
Cognate with 'twelve'. 'Twaalf uur' is both noon and midnight; add 's middags or 's nachts to be clear.
Note the vowel change from 'drie' to 'der-', just like English three/thirteen. Then veertien (14), vijftien, zestien, zeventien, achttien, negentien.
The ending '-tig' matches English '-ty'. It is pronounced 'tuch' with the throat sound, not 'tig'.
Dutch says the units first, like old English 'four-and-twenty blackbirds': een-en-twintig. All numbers up to 99 work this way, written as one word.

example.en: My sister is twenty-one years old.

note: Again 'der-' as in 'dertien'. The remaining tens are regular: vijftig (50), zestig, zeventig, tachtig (80, note the t-), negentig.
Spelled with 'veer-' not 'vier-', like English forty/four. Many speakers pronounce the v of veertig as 'f'.
No 'een' is needed: 'honderd euro' = a hundred euros. 'Tweehonderd', 'driehonderd' etc. are written as one word.
Cognate with 'thousand'. Dutch uses a dot as thousands separator and a comma for decimals: 1.000,50.

example.en: The bike costs a thousand euros.

note: Irregular, like English 'first'. Ordinals are written '1e' or '1ste'. 'De eerste keer' = the first time.
Regular: number + '-de' (tweede, vierde, vijfde). 'Tweedehands' = second-hand.
Irregular (not 'driede'). From 20 upwards ordinals take '-ste': twintigste, honderdste.
Careful with time: 'half drie' is 2:30 (half way to three), not 3:30. 'De helft' is the noun 'the half'.
Means 'a few', not strictly two. 'Een paar schoenen' can mean a pair of shoes or a few shoes, context decides.

example.en: I am staying a few days.

note: Means the wider family (relatives). The household unit of parents and children is 'het gezin'. Stress on the 'li'.
Cognate with 'mother'. 'Oe' is the Dutch spelling of the 'oo' sound in 'moon'. Children say 'mama' or 'mam'.
Cognate with 'father'. Informal: 'papa', 'pap' or 'pa'. 'Vaderland' is the fatherland, as in the Dutch anthem.
Plural of 'ouder' (older); compare English 'elders'. 'Grootouders' = grandparents.
Cognate with 'son'. Plural 'zonen' or 'zoons'. 'Zoontje' is a little son.
Cognate with 'daughter'; the 'ch' is the throat sound. Plural 'dochters'.
Same as German 'Kind', related to English 'kin'. Irregular plural 'kinderen'. 'Kindje' (little child) and all diminutives are 'het' words.
Cognate with 'brother'; the fuller form 'broeder' is now mostly used for monks and nurses. 'Broertje' = little brother.
Short form of 'zuster', which is now used for nurses and nuns, like 'broeder'. 'Zusje' = little sister.
Everyday word for grandfather; the formal term is 'grootvader'. Plural 'opa's' with an apostrophe, as with all nouns ending in -a.
Everyday word for grandmother; formal 'grootmoeder'. Flemish families often say 'bomma' and 'bompa' instead.

example.en: Grandma bakes apple pie every Sunday.

note: Related to Latin 'avunculus' through the same old Germanic root that gave English 'eme'. 'Ome Jan' is a folksy way to say Uncle Jan.
Borrowed from French 'tante'. Two syllables: 'tan-tuh'.
'Mijn man' = my husband. Plural 'mannen'. 'Echtgenoot' is the formal word for husband.
'Mijn vrouw' = my wife. Cognate with German 'Frau'. 'Mevrouw' (Mrs, ma'am) is built on it.
'Mijn vriend / vriendin' usually means boyfriend / girlfriend; for a plain friend say 'een vriend van me'. Cognate with 'friend'.

example.target: Zij is een goede vriendin van mij.
example.en: She is a good friend of mine.

note: Borrowed from English, pronounced 'bay-bee'. Plural 'baby's' with an apostrophe (Dutch rule for words ending in -y).
From 'jong' (young). Plural 'jongens', also used as 'guys' when addressing a group: 'Hé jongens!'
A diminutive of the old word 'meid', so it takes 'het' even though it refers to a female. Plural 'meisjes'.

example.target: Het meisje speelt in de tuin.
example.en: The girl is playing in the garden.

note: Plural of 'de mens' (human being). All plurals take 'de'. Related to German 'Mensch'; English borrowed 'mensch' via Yiddish.
'Buur' = neighbour, so buurman / buurvrouw. The plural for neighbours in general is 'de buren'. 'De buurt' is the neighbourhood.
Cognate with 'king'. The Netherlands and Belgium are both monarchies; Koningsdag (27 April) is the Dutch national holiday.
Covers both nephew and male cousin; 'de nicht' is both niece and female cousin. Context tells you which.
Grandchild is 'small child'; 'kleinzoon' and 'kleindochter' follow the same pattern, mirroring 'grootouders'.
From Latin 'persona'. Plural 'personen', used on signs and tickets: 'voor 4 personen'. In everyday speech 'mens' is more common.
Cognate with 'bread'; 'oo' is a long 'oh'. 'Broodje' is a bread roll or sandwich. Dutch lunch is traditionally bread.

example.target: Ik koop vers brood bij de bakker.
example.en: I buy fresh bread at the baker's.

literal: butter + 'ham' (an old word of unclear origin, not the meat)
note: A single slice of bread, usually buttered and topped. 'Boterhammen' are the standard Dutch lunch and school meal.
Cognate with 'cheese'. Gouda and Edam are named after Dutch towns; the Netherlands is one of the largest cheese exporters in the world.
Irregular plural 'eieren'. 'Ei' sounds the same as 'ij' in Dutch. 'Eitje' = little egg, also slang for something easy.
Cognate with 'apple'. 'Aardappel' (earth apple) is a potato and 'sinaasappel' (China's apple) is an orange.
Cognate with 'milk'. 'Karnemelk' is buttermilk, a traditional Dutch lunch drink. Flemish and dialect often say 'melluk'.
Spelled exactly as in English but pronounced 'vah-ter'. 'Kraanwater' is tap water, which is excellent and free to ask for.

example.en: May I have a glass of water?

note: The Dutch are among the world's biggest coffee drinkers. 'Koffie verkeerd' (coffee wrong) is a milky coffee; 'een bakje' is slang for a cup.
The Dutch East India Company brought tea to Europe in the 1600s; the 'th' spelling is a leftover, pronounced simply 't'.
Cognate with 'beer'. 'Een biertje' (a little beer) is how you order one; 'een pilsje' is a lager.
From Latin 'vinum', like English 'wine'. 'Rode wijn', 'witte wijn'. English 'brandy' comes from Dutch 'brandewijn' (burnt wine).
Same idea as French 'pomme de terre'. Potatoes are the traditional base of Dutch dinner; 'stamppot' is mashed potato with vegetables.
From 'groen' (green). Usually collective: 'groente eten'. Plural 'groenten' or 'groentes'.
Collective, like English; a single piece is 'een vrucht'. Pronounced with the tricky 'ui' sound, somewhere between 'ow' and 'oy'.
Cognate with 'flesh'. 'Vleeswaren' are cold cuts; 'gehakt' is minced meat.
Both the bird and the meat. 'Kipfilet' = chicken breast. 'Kippenvel' (chicken skin) means goosebumps.
Cognate with 'fish'. Raw herring, 'haring', is the classic Dutch street snack, eaten with onions.

example.target: Ik eet liever vis dan vlees.

note: 'Rijsttafel' (rice table) is the Dutch-Indonesian feast of many small dishes, a legacy of the colonial era.
'Erwtensoep' (split-pea soup, also 'snert') is the classic winter dish, thick enough for a spoon to stand up in.
Pronounced 'sow-ker' with the 'ui' sound. 'Suiker en melk?' is what you get asked with coffee.
Cognate with 'salt'. 'Drop', the famous Dutch liquorice, often comes 'zout' (salty) and surprises foreigners.
Cognate with 'butter'. 'Pindakaas' (peanut cheese) is peanut butter, because 'boter' was a protected name.
Diminutive of 'koek' (cake). English 'cookie' comes from this word via Dutch settlers in New York. Diminutives always take 'het'.

example.target: Wil je een koekje bij de koffie?
example.en: Would you like a biscuit with your coffee?

note: Two thin waffles with caramel syrup in between, originally from Gouda. Put it on your hot coffee cup to soften it. English 'waffle' is from Dutch 'wafel'.
The word in most of the Netherlands; in Flanders and the southern Netherlands it is 'friet' or 'frietjes'. 'Patatje met' = fries with mayonnaise.
From French; the final -t is pronounced in Dutch unlike in French. An 'eetcafé' is a pub that serves meals.
A Dutch 'café' is really a pub or bar, serving beer as much as coffee. A 'bruin café' (brown café) is a cosy old pub with dark wood.
Ask for 'de kaart'. 'Het menu' on its own usually means a set menu of several courses.
From German 'Oberkellner' (head waiter). Calling 'Ober!' is old-fashioned; just catch their eye. Female staff: 'serveerster'.
From 'rekenen' (to calculate), cognate with 'reckon'. Also means a bank account ('bankrekening').
Service is included in the Netherlands; rounding up or 5-10% is a normal tip. 'Fooi geven' = to tip.
From 'ontbijten' (to breakfast); the '-bijt' part is related to 'bite'. Typically bread with cheese or 'hagelslag' (chocolate sprinkles).
Borrowed from English; the verb is 'lunchen'. The older Dutch word 'middageten' is still heard. Flemish often says 'het middagmaal'.
The Dutch eat dinner early, often around 6 pm. 'Diner' is a more formal word for a dinner out.

example.en: What are we having for dinner tonight?

note: Any outdoor seating at a café. 'Op het terras zitten' and 'een terrasje pakken' (grab a little terrace) are national pastimes on the first sunny day.
From Latin 'prosit', like German 'Prost'. Custom is to look each person in the eye as you clink. 'Santé' is also common in Flanders.
Said before eating, like 'bon appétit'. 'Smakelijk' is from 'smaak' (taste), cognate with English 'smack' as in 'smack your lips'.
The simplest polite way to order: 'Mag ik een koffie?'. From 'mogen' (may, to be allowed). Add 'alstublieft' for extra politeness.

example.target: Mag ik een thee met melk?
example.en: May I have a tea with milk?

note: 'Graag' softens 'ik wil' (I want) into a polite 'I'd like'. In Flanders 'ik had graag ...' is common too.

literal: the bill, if it pleases you
note: Or 'Mag ik afrekenen?' (may I settle up?). Many places prefer you to pay at the bar, and some take cards only ('alleen pinnen').
Regular verb: past 'bestelde', participle 'besteld'. 'De bestelling' is the order. Verbs with be- never add ge- in the participle.
Cognate with 'glass'. Plural 'glazen' (s becomes z). 'Een glaasje' = a small glass, often of something alcoholic.
Cognate with 'flask'. Plural 'flessen'. 'Een flesje water' = a small bottle of water.
Diminutive of 'de kop' (cup, also 'head' informally). Coffee and tea nearly always come as 'een kopje'. 'Een kop koffie' is also fine.
From French. Regular: 'reserveerde', 'gereserveerd'. 'Een tafel reserveren' = to book a table.

example.target: Ik wil een tafel reserveren voor twee personen.
example.en: I would like to book a table for two.

note: 'Hoofd' (head, main) + 'gerecht' (dish). 'Voorgerecht' = starter, 'nagerecht' = dessert. 'Gerecht' also means a court of law.

example.target: Als hoofdgerecht neem ik de vis.
example.en: For the main course I will have the fish.

note: Informal word for dessert, from 'toe' (in addition), so a 'little something on top'. The menu will say 'nagerecht' or 'dessert'.
Cognate with 'board'. Also means a sign or a blackboard ('schoolbord'). Plural 'borden'.
Originally a small glass of jenever (Dutch gin); now also an informal drinks gathering, often with snacks ('borrelhapjes'). 'Vrijdagmiddagborrel' = Friday drinks.
Dutch asks whether a seat is free, not whether it is taken. 'Vrij' (free) is cognate with 'free'; 'bezet' = taken.
Same as German 'Reise'. 'Goede reis!' = have a good trip. Plural 'reizen', which is also the verb.

example.target: Goede reis en tot volgende week!
example.en: Have a good trip and see you next week!

note: Regular: past 'reisde', participle 'gereisd'. Note the s/z switch: 'ik reis' but 'wij reizen'. 'Reiziger' = traveller.
From French 'vacances'. 'Op vakantie gaan' = to go on holiday. 'Fijne vakantie!' = have a nice holiday.

example.target: We gaan in augustus op vakantie.
example.en: We are going on holiday in August.

note: Pronounced 'pas-port'. Dutch citizens over 14 must carry ID; an 'identiteitskaart' (ID card) also counts.
From French; stress on the last syllable. Plural 'hotels'.
One word for map, playing card, menu card, postcard and ticket. 'Kaartje' (little card) is a ticket; 'landkaart' makes the map explicit.
'Linksaf' = turn left; 'aan de linkerkant' = on the left side. In politics 'links' is the left wing, as in English.
'Rechtsaf' = turn right. 'Recht' alone means 'straight' or 'law/right', so 'rechts' is specifically the direction.
'Recht' (straight) + 'door' (through). Don't confuse with 'rechts' (right). 'Ga rechtdoor' = go straight on.

example.en: Go straight ahead and then right.

note: Cognate with 'street', both from Latin 'strata'. Street names are written as one word: Kerkstraat, Hoofdstraat.
Cognate with 'hook'. 'Om de hoek' = around the corner; 'op de hoek' = on the corner.
Cognate with 'far'. 'Hoe ver is het?' = how far is it? Inflected form 'verre'; 'verder' = further, also used for 'next'.
'Dicht' means close/shut and 'bij' means by/near. 'Hier dichtbij' = near here. 'Vlakbij' is a close synonym.
'Waar' is cognate with 'where'. Plural: 'Waar zijn ...?'. 'Waar is het toilet?' is probably the most useful sentence in this pack.
Cognate with 'way'. As an adverb 'weg' means 'away/gone': 'hij is weg'. 'De weg vragen' = to ask the way; 'snelweg' = motorway.
Cognate with 'bridge'. Amsterdam has over 1,500 bridges; 'ophaalbrug' is a drawbridge. Plural 'bruggen'.
From Latin. Road signs say 'Centrum'. 'De binnenstad' (inner city) means the same historic centre.
'In' + 'gang' (going, passage). The 'g' in 'gang' is the throat sound. 'Geen ingang' = no entry.
'Uit' (out) + 'gang'. 'Nooduitgang' = emergency exit. On the motorway an exit is 'afslag' or 'afrit'.
Pronounced 'twa-let'. 'De wc' (pronounced 'way-say') is just as common. Cafés may charge 50 cents for non-customers.
From French 'coffre' (chest). 'Koffers pakken' = to pack your bags. 'Kofferbak' is the boot/trunk of a car.
'Ver-' (astray) + 'dwalen' (to wander). Regular: 'verdwaalde'. The result is said with 'zijn': 'ik ben verdwaald' = I am lost.
A city canal, as in Amsterdam's 'grachtengordel' (canal belt). A countryside canal is 'een kanaal'. Related to 'graven' (to dig).
From French 'rotonde'. The Netherlands is full of them; traffic already on the roundabout usually has priority.
Like German 'Grenze'. Plural 'grenzen'. 'Over de grens' = across the border; 'grenzeloos' = boundless.
The origin of 'fiets' is a famous unsolved puzzle in Dutch etymology. The Netherlands has more bikes than people. 'Fietsje' = little bike.
Regular: 'fietste', 'gefietst'. The Dutch cycle in all weather; 'tegen de wind in fietsen' (cycling into the wind) is the national workout.

example.target: Ik fiets elke dag naar mijn werk.
example.en: I cycle to work every day.

note: Pronounced 'ow-to'. Plural 'auto's' with an apostrophe, the Dutch rule for words ending in a long vowel. 'Autosnelweg' = motorway.
Borrowed from English 'train' in the 1800s; 'ei' sounds like 'ay'. NS (Nederlandse Spoorwegen) runs the yellow-and-blue trains.

example.target: De trein naar Rotterdam vertrekt om acht uur.
example.en: The train to Rotterdam leaves at eight.

note: Plural 'bussen'. Also means a tin or can ('een bus koekjes'). 'Bushalte' = bus stop.
Pronounced 'trem' in the Netherlands and 'tram' (as in English) in Flanders. Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht all have trams.
Only Amsterdam and Rotterdam have one. Plural 'metro's'. From French 'métro'.
Pronounced 'sta-SHON', French-style. 'Centraal Station' is the main station in most big cities. Plural 'stations'.
'Vliegen' (to fly) + 'tuig' (gear, craft). Invented as a native word instead of borrowing. Plural 'vliegtuigen'.
The everyday word; 'luchthaven' (air harbour) is the official one. Schiphol, near Amsterdam, lies about 4 metres below sea level.

example.target: Hoe kom ik op het vliegveld?
example.en: How do I get to the airport?

note: Cognate with 'boat' ('oo' = long 'oh'). Plural 'boten'. English took 'yacht' from Dutch 'jacht' and 'skipper' from 'schipper'.
Diminutive of 'kaart', so 'het'. Used for train, bus, cinema and museum tickets. 'Een retourtje' = a return ticket; 'enkele reis' = single.
'OV' stands for 'openbaar vervoer' (public transport). You check in and out by holding it to a reader; forgetting to check out costs you money.
From French. 'Spoor' (track) is what the signs and announcements use: 'de trein vertrekt van spoor 4'.
Related to 'halt'. 'Bushalte', 'tramhalte'. 'Volgende halte' = next stop, heard in every tram announcement.
Covers both driving and riding, cognate with 'ride'. Strong verb: past 'reed', participle 'gereden'. 'Rijbewijs' = driving licence.
Strong verb: past 'vertrok', participle 'vertrokken' (with 'zijn'). 'Vertrek' is the departure, as on airport boards.
Separable verb: the 'aan' goes to the end of the sentence ('ik kom om tien uur aan'). Strong past 'kwam aan', participle 'aangekomen'. 'Aankomst' = arrival.

example.target: De trein komt om half zes aan.
example.en: The train arrives at half past five.

note: 'Pad' is cognate with 'path'. The country has about 35,000 km of them, usually red asphalt. Pedestrians who stray onto one get a bell rung at them.
Plural 'taxi's' with an apostrophe. Dutch taxis are expensive; the metro and bike are the usual alternatives.
From French 'file' (line, queue) and pronounced the French way, 'feel'. Radio traffic reports list the day's 'files' in kilometres.

example.target: Er staat een lange file op de A2.
example.en: There is a long traffic jam on the A2.

note: Strong verb: past 'liep', participle 'gelopen'. Careful: in Flanders 'lopen' means to run; walking there is 'wandelen' or 'stappen'. Cognate with 'leap'.

example.en: We are walking to the centre.

note: Separable: 'ik stap in Utrecht over'. Regular past 'stapte over', participle 'overgestapt'. Also 'instappen' (get on) and 'uitstappen' (get off).

example.en: You have to change in Utrecht.

note: From 'traag' (slow). 'Tien minuten vertraging' is what the station sign shows. Related adjective 'traag' is more common in Flanders than 'langzaam'.
'Parkeren' is to park. 'Parkeergarage' = multi-storey car park. City-centre parking is expensive; 'P+R' lots on the edge are the cheap option.
Cognate with 'tide' (as in 'time and tide'). 'Op tijd' = on time; 'geen tijd' = no time. 'Tijdje' = a little while.
Cognate with 'hour'. After a number it stays singular: 'twee uur' = two hours or two o'clock. Plural 'uren'.
Plural 'minuten'. 'Een minuutje' = just a moment. 'Vijf over twee' = five past two.
Plural 'dagen' (short a becomes long). 'Dagje uit' = a day out. 'Dag!' on its own is a greeting or goodbye.
Cognate with 'week', pronounced 'vayk'. 'Volgende week' = next week; 'vorige week' = last week. Plural 'weken'.
Cognate with 'month' and 'maan' (moon). Plural 'maanden'. Month names are not capitalised in Dutch.
Cognate with 'year' (Dutch j = English y). After a number it stays singular: 'twintig jaar'. Plural 'jaren'. 'Nieuwjaar' = New Year.

example.target: Ik woon hier al drie jaar.
example.en: I have lived here for three years.

note: From 'van' (of) + 'daag', an old form of 'dag'. Compare 'vanavond' (tonight), 'vanmorgen' (this morning), 'vannacht' (tonight/last night).
Means both 'tomorrow' and 'morning', just like German 'morgen/Morgen'. 'Morgenochtend' = tomorrow morning. 'Tot morgen!' = see you tomorrow.

example.target: Morgen ga ik naar Den Haag.
example.en: Tomorrow I am going to The Hague.

note: Cognate with 'yesterday' and German 'gestern'. 'Eergisteren' = the day before yesterday; 'overmorgen' = the day after tomorrow.
Days are not capitalised in Dutch. 'Op maandag' = on Monday; 'maandags' or ''s maandags' = on Mondays.
The odd one out: it is related to Tuesday but through a different form of the Germanic god's name. Pronounced 'dins-dach'.
Named after Wodan (Odin), exactly like English Wednesday. 'Oe' is pronounced 'oo'. Many Dutch primary schools finish early on Wednesday.
'Donder' = thunder, the god Donar (Thor). 'Donderdag' is a common day for late-night shopping ('koopavond').
Named after the goddess Frija, as in English. Looks like 'vrij' (free), which makes it easy to remember.
From Saturn, like English Saturday (German instead has 'Samstag'). The big weekly market day in many towns.
'Zon' = sun. Most shops used to close on Sundays; in big cities 'koopzondag' (shopping Sunday) is now normal.
'Vanochtend' = this morning; ''s ochtends' = in the mornings (the 's is an old genitive 'des'). 'Morgen' can also mean morning.
Despite the literal meaning, 'middag' is the whole afternoon, 12 to about 6. ''s Middags' = in the afternoon. Noon itself is 'twaalf uur'.
Cognate with 'evening' and German 'Abend'. 'Vanavond' = tonight (this evening); ''s avonds' = in the evening.
Cognate with 'night'; the 'ch' is the throat sound. ''s Nachts' = at night; 'vannacht' = tonight (late) or last night.
Dutch asks 'how late'. Answer: 'Het is drie uur' (3:00), 'kwart over drie' (3:15), 'half vier' (3:30!), 'kwart voor vier' (3:45).
The classic trap: 'half drie' is 2:30, halfway to three. 'Tien voor half drie' = 2:20 and 'tien over half drie' = 2:40 are normal ways to tell the time.

example.target: De les begint om half drie.
example.en: The lesson starts at half past two.

note: Months are lowercase and close to English: januari, februari, maart, april, mei, juni, juli, augustus, september, oktober, november, december.
Borrowed from English, pronounced the Dutch way ('vee-kent'). 'Fijn weekend!' = have a nice weekend. 'In het weekend' = at the weekend.

example.en: What are you doing this weekend?

note: From French 'couleur'. 'Welke kleur?' = which colour? 'Kleuren' is also the verb 'to colour'. 'Kleurrijk' = colourful.
Cognate with 'red'. Adjectives add -e before a noun: 'rode wijn' (the d doubles the vowel sound, so one o). 'Roodkapje' = Little Red Riding Hood.

example.target: Ik wil graag een glas rode wijn.
example.en: I would like a glass of red wine.

note: The national colour, from the royal House of Oranje-Nassau. The fruit is 'sinaasappel', not oranje. The football team is simply 'Oranje'.

example.en: On King's Day everyone wears orange.

note: Cognate with 'yellow' (Dutch g for English y, as in 'gisteren'/yesterday). Before a noun: 'gele'. Dutch trains are yellow.
Cognate with 'green'. 'Groente' (vegetables) comes from it. Also 'inexperienced', like English: 'een groentje' is a rookie.
Cognate with 'blue'; 'auw' sounds like 'ow'. 'Een blauwtje lopen' (to walk a little blue one) means to be turned down romantically.
The everyday word; 'purper' exists but is literary. 'Paarse krokodil' (purple crocodile) is Dutch shorthand for absurd bureaucracy, from a famous advert.
From French 'rose'. Two syllables: 'roh-zuh'. It does not change before a noun: 'een roze jas'.
Cognate with 'brown', with the 'ui' sound. 'Bruin brood' = brown bread; a 'bruin café' is a traditional pub.
Related to English 'swarthy'. 'Zwart werken' = to work off the books. 'Zwart-wit' = black and white.
Cognate with 'white'. Before a noun: 'witte' (double t keeps the i short). 'Witte wijn', 'wittebrood'.
Cognate with 'grey'. Before a noun: 'grijze' (s becomes z). 'Grijs haar' = grey hair. The standard colour of Dutch skies.
Like English 'light', it covers pale colours, low weight and the noun 'het licht'. 'Lichtblauw' = light blue. Cognate, with the 'ch' throat sound.
'Donkerblauw' = dark blue; 'het is donker' = it is dark. Related to German 'dunkel'. 'In het donker' = in the dark.

example.target: In december wordt het vroeg donker.
example.en: In December it gets dark early.

note: Cognate with 'form'. 'In vorm zijn' = to be in shape. Plural 'vormen'. 'Vormgeving' = design.
From Latin 'circulus'. The 'c' is pronounced 's' before i and e. A social or traffic circle is 'kring' or 'rotonde', not 'cirkel'.
'Vier' (four) + 'kant' (side, edge). As an adjective 'vierkant' = square-shaped. A town square is 'het plein', not vierkant.
'Drie' + 'hoek' (corner). The same pattern gives 'vijfhoek' (pentagon) and 'zeshoek' (hexagon).
Also a bus or tram route ('lijn 2') and a diet ('aan de lijn'). 'Lijntje' = a short line. 'Luchtlijn' = airline.
Plural 'stippen'. 'Stippellijn' = dotted line. A 'stip aan de horizon' (dot on the horizon) is a long-term goal.
Cognate with 'round'. Also a preposition 'around': 'rond de tafel'. 'Rondje' = a round of drinks or a short loop walk.
Cognate with 'star'. Plural 'sterren'. 'Sterrenbeeld' = constellation or star sign; 'filmster' = film star.
Cognate with 'heart'. Plural 'harten'. 'Hartje' is a little heart (emoji). 'Hartelijk' = heartfelt, as in 'hartelijk bedankt'.
'Recht' (straight, right) + 'hoek' (corner, angle). Adjective 'rechthoekig' = rectangular.
Cognate with 'stripe'. Plural 'strepen'. 'Gestreept' = striped. 'Een streep zetten onder' = to draw a line under something.
Related to German 'Leichnam' (corpse) and to 'lijk' (corpse) + an old word for 'covering'. 'Lichamelijk' = physical. 'Lijf' is the informal word for body.
Cognate with 'head' (and German 'Haupt'). 'Hoofd-' as a prefix means 'main': hoofdstad (capital), hoofdstraat. Informal: 'de kop'.
Plural 'ogen' (one o, long sound). 'Oogarts' = eye doctor. 'In het oog houden' = to keep an eye on.
Cognate with 'ear'. Plural 'oren'. 'Oorbel' (ear bell) = earring. 'Oorpijn' = earache.
Cognate with 'nose'. 'Eu' sounds roughly like the vowel in French 'deux'. 'Neusje van de zalm' (nose of the salmon) = the best bit.
Cognate with 'mouth'. 'Mondkapje' = face mask. 'Hou je mond!' = shut up (literally: hold your mouth).
Cognate with 'tooth' (d for th). Plural 'tanden'. 'Tandarts' (tooth doctor) = dentist; 'tandpasta' = toothpaste.

example.target: Ik heb pijn aan mijn tand.

note: Spelled like English; plural 'handen'. 'Handschoen' (hand shoe) = glove. 'Een handje helpen' = to lend a hand.
Same as English; plural 'armen'. As an adjective 'arm' means 'poor' (cognate with German 'arm'). 'Armband' = bracelet.
False friend: 'been' means leg, though it is cognate with 'bone' (and can still mean bone, as in 'beenderen'). Plural 'benen'.
Cognate with 'foot'. Plural 'voeten'. 'Te voet' = on foot; 'voetbal' = football; 'voetpad' = footpath.
The everyday word for stomach/belly ('buikpijn' = stomach ache). 'De maag' is the organ itself. 'Ui' sound again.

example.en: My daughter has a stomach ache.

note: Cognate with 'ridge' and German 'Rücken'. 'Rugzak' (back sack) = backpack. 'Rugpijn' = back pain.
Cognate with 'hair'. Also the pronoun 'haar' = her. 'Mijn haar is nat' = my hair is wet. 'Kapper' = hairdresser.
'Arts' = doctor (physician); 'dokter' is the informal word. You must be registered with a 'huisarts' to see a specialist.

example.target: Ik heb een afspraak bij de huisarts.
example.en: I have an appointment with the GP.

note: 'Zieken' (sick people) + 'huis'. German has the same idea with 'Krankenhaus'. Plural 'ziekenhuizen'.
Cognate with 'sick'. 'Ziek zijn' = to be ill; 'zich ziek melden' = to call in sick. 'Ziekte' = illness.

example.target: Ik ben ziek, ik blijf thuis.
example.en: I am ill, I am staying home.

note: Cognate with English 'sound' (as in 'safe and sound') and German 'gesund'. 'Gezondheid' = health, also said after a sneeze.
Cognate with 'pain', both from Latin 'poena'. Combine freely: hoofdpijn, buikpijn, keelpijn (sore throat). 'Pijn doen' = to hurt.
'Koorts hebben' = to have a fever. 'Hooikoorts' = hay fever. The thermometer in the Netherlands reads 'graden Celsius'.
From Greek 'apotheke' (storehouse), like German 'Apotheke'. For prescriptions; a 'drogist' sells over-the-counter remedies and toiletries.
Plural 'medicijnen'. Stress on the last syllable. 'Medicijnen slikken' = to take medication. The science is 'geneeskunde'.
An adjective: 'ik ben verkouden' = I have a cold. Built on 'koud' (cold). The noun is 'verkoudheid'.

example.target: Hij is al een week verkouden.
example.en: He has had a cold for a week.

note: Cognate with 'knee', but in Dutch the k is pronounced: 'k-nee'. Plural 'knieën' with a diaeresis.
'Hoofd' + 'pijn'. 'Ik heb hoofdpijn' (no article). The Dutch word for a hangover headache is 'een kater' (a tomcat).
Cognate with 'house', with the 'ui' sound. 'Thuis' = at home. Plural 'huizen'. 'Huisje' = little house or holiday cottage.

example.target: Ik ben om zes uur thuis.

note: From Latin 'camera', like English 'chamber'. Plural 'kamers'. 'Op kamers wonen' = to live in student digs.
Cognate with 'kitchen', both from Latin 'coquina'. 'De Hollandse keuken' also means Dutch cuisine.
'Bad' = bath, cognate. In Dutch homes the toilet is often a separate little room, 'de wc', not in the bathroom.
From 'slapen' (to sleep). Room names are compounds: slaapkamer, badkamer, woonkamer, eetkamer, kinderkamer.
From 'wonen' (to live, reside). 'Huiskamer' is an older synonym. Traditionally with big front windows and no curtains drawn.
Cognate with 'door'. Plural 'deuren'. 'Voordeur' = front door; 'achterdeur' = back door. 'Deurtje' = little door.
Plural 'ramen'. 'Venster' is the older word, now common in Flanders and in 'vensterbank' (windowsill). 'Raam' also means frame.
From Latin 'tabula', like 'table'. 'Aan tafel!' = dinner is ready. 'Tafeltje' = small table.

example.target: De sleutels liggen op de tafel.
example.en: The keys are on the table.

note: Cognate with 'stool' but means an ordinary chair. A stool is 'een kruk'. Plural 'stoelen'. 'Rolstoel' = wheelchair.
Same as English. 'Naar bed gaan' = to go to bed; 'in bed liggen' = to lie in bed. Plural 'bedden'.
One word for sofa, bench and bank; context decides. 'Op de bank hangen' = to lounge on the sofa. Flemish often says 'de zetel'.
Any cupboard, closet or wardrobe. 'Kledingkast' = wardrobe; 'koelkast' = fridge; 'boekenkast' = bookcase. 'Kastje' = small cabinet.
Same as English. 'Het licht aandoen' = to switch the light on. 'Lampje' = small lamp or indicator light.
From 'sluiten' (to lock, close). Plural 'sleutels'. 'Sleutelbos' = bunch of keys. 'Huissleutel' = house key.
False friend: not a trap (that is 'een val'). Related to 'trappen' (to step, kick). Dutch stairs are famously steep and narrow.
Cognate with English 'town' and German 'Zaun' (fence): originally an enclosed plot. 'Tuinieren' = to garden. 'Ui' sound.
Cognate with 'floor'. A storey is 'de verdieping': 'eerste verdieping' is the first floor above the ground floor ('begane grond').
To live somewhere; 'leven' is to be alive. Regular: 'woonde', 'gewoond'. 'Woning' = dwelling; 'woonkamer' = living room.
From French, pronounced 'doosh'. 'Douchen' = to shower. Dutch showers are short: hot water and energy are expensive.
'Koel' (cool) + 'kast'. The freezer is 'de vriezer' or 'diepvries'. 'IJskast' (ice cupboard) is an older word still heard.
Cognate with English 'thatch' and German 'Dach'. Plural 'daken'. 'Dakterras' = roof terrace.
Stress on the last syllable. Plural 'balkons'. In Dutch flats a balcony is often the only outdoor space, used for 'balkonnetje zitten'.
From Latin 'speculum', like German 'Spiegel'. 'Spiegelei' (mirror egg) = fried egg sunny side up.
Borrowed from English but pronounced 'flet'; it means both the apartment and the whole block. 'Appartement' is the smarter word.

example.target: Ze woont in een flat in Rotterdam.
example.en: She lives in a flat in Rotterdam.

note: Plural only, a contraction of 'klederen'. 'Kleding' is the collective 'clothing'. 'Kleren maken de man' = clothes make the man.
Any coat or jacket. Plural 'jassen'. 'Regenjas' = raincoat; 'winterjas' = winter coat. 'Jasje' = a suit jacket.

example.target: Doe je jas aan, het is koud.
example.en: Put your coat on, it is cold.

note: Singular in Dutch: 'een broek' = a pair of trousers. Cognate with 'breeches'. 'Korte broek' = shorts.
Named after the metal rivets ('spijkers' = nails). 'Jeans' is also used. Dutch people wear jeans everywhere, including the office.
Borrowed from English, with a hyphen. 'Het shirt' is also used for any shirt. Plural 'T-shirts'.
'Ui' sound. Plural 'truien'. 'Coltrui' = turtleneck; 'foute kersttrui' = ugly Christmas jumper.
Plural 'jurken'. 'Jurkje' is a little dress. Flemish often says 'kleed' or 'kleedje' instead, which in the Netherlands means a rug.
Same word as German 'Rock' (skirt). Plural 'rokken'. 'Rokje' = short skirt.
Cognate with 'shoe'; 'sch' is 's' + the throat sound. Plural 'schoenen'. Children put their 'schoen' by the chimney for Sinterklaas.
Cognate with 'sock'. Plural 'sokken'. 'Er de sokken in zetten' = to hurry up.
Cognate with 'hood' and 'hat'. Plural 'hoeden'. 'Hoedje' = little hat. 'Hoeden' is also the verb 'to guard'.
A baseball or flat cap. Plural 'petten'. 'Dat gaat boven mijn pet' (that goes above my cap) = that is beyond me.
Same origin as 'shawl', from Persian via French 'châle'. 'Sj' is the Dutch spelling of the 'sh' sound.
A glove is a 'shoe for the hand', like German 'Handschuh'. Plural 'handschoenen'. 'Wanten' are mittens.
'Onder' (under) + 'goed' (goods, stuff). 'Onderbroek' = underpants; 'beha' = bra (from the initials of 'bustehouder').
Singular in Dutch: 'een bril' = a pair of glasses. From 'beril' (beryl), the crystal early lenses were made from. 'Zonnebril' = sunglasses.
Any bag: handbag, shopping bag, school bag. Plural 'tassen'. 'Tasje' = a small (plastic) bag; shops charge for one.
Both 'wear' and 'carry', like French 'porter'. Strong verb: past 'droeg', participle 'gedragen'. Cognate with 'drag'.

example.en: She is wearing a red dress.

note: Separable: 'ik trek mijn jas aan'. Strong: past 'trok aan', participle 'aangetrokken'. Also means 'to attract'.
The opposite of 'aantrekken', also separable: 'ik trek mijn schoenen uit'. Past 'trok uit', participle 'uitgetrokken'.
'Het past' = it fits; 'mag ik dit passen?' = may I try this on? Also 'passen op' = to look after. Regular: 'paste', 'gepast'.
Clothing size: 'welke maat heeft u?'. Also means 'measure' and, informally, 'mate, buddy' ('maatje'). Dutch sizes are European numbers.
Both a button and a knot (cognate with 'knot'). Plural 'knopen'. 'Knoopje' = small button; 'een knoop doorhakken' = to make a decision.
Short for 'ritssluiting'. 'De rits dichtdoen' = to zip up. Plural 'ritsen'.
Also a strap or a rowing oar. 'Veiligheidsriem' or 'gordel' = seat belt. Plural 'riemen'.
Cognate with 'work'. 'Naar mijn werk' = to work (the place). 'Aan het werk' = at work. 'Werkloos' = unemployed.
Regular: 'werkte', 'gewerkt'. 'Werken bij' = to work at (a company). The Dutch have one of the shortest average working weeks in Europe.

example.target: Ik werk vier dagen per week.
example.en: I work four days a week.

note: 'Een baan zoeken' = to look for a job. Also means a lane or track ('rijbaan', 'ijsbaan' = ice rink). 'Bijbaan' = side job.
From French 'comptoir' (counter). 'Op kantoor' = at the office. 'Thuiswerken' (working from home) is very common.
English 'boss' was borrowed from this word by Dutch settlers in America. Plural 'bazen'. 'Bazig' = bossy.
Same form for men and women. Plural 'collega's' with an apostrophe. Stress on 'le'.
From 'leren' (to teach/learn). 'Lerares' is the female form; 'docent' is used at secondary and higher level, 'juf' and 'meester' in primary school.
From 'leren' + '-ling' (person), like 'jongeling'. For school pupils; also an apprentice. Plural 'leerlingen'.
Used for higher education only; school pupils are 'leerlingen'. Stress on the last syllable. 'Studentenstad' = university town.
Cognate with 'school'. 'Basisschool' = primary school; 'middelbare school' = secondary school. Plural 'scholen'.
Stress on '-teit'. Leiden (1575) is the oldest in the Netherlands, Leuven (1425) in Flanders. A 'hogeschool' is a university of applied sciences.
From French 'leçon'. Plural 'lessen'. 'Les geven' = to teach; 'les hebben' = to have class. 'Rijles' = driving lesson.

example.target: De les begint om negen uur.

note: Means both 'learn' and 'teach' ('ik leer hem Nederlands'). Regular: 'leerde', 'geleerd'. 'Geleerde' = a scholar.
To be enrolled in or to study a subject at university: 'ik studeer geneeskunde'. For revising, Dutch says 'leren'. Regular: 'studeerde'.
Cognate with 'book' ('oe' = 'oo'). Plural 'boeken'. 'Boekje' = booklet. 'Boeken' is also the verb 'to book'.
Same as English. Plural 'pennen'. 'Potlood' = pencil (literally 'pot lead').
Plural 'examens'. 'Examen doen' = to sit an exam; 'slagen' = to pass, 'zakken' = to fail. 'Tentamen' is a university course exam.
'Huis' + 'werk', like English 'homework'. Always singular: 'huiswerk maken' = to do homework.
From 'vergaderen' (to meet, assemble), related to 'gaderen' (to gather). The Dutch 'vergadercultuur' (meeting culture) is a running joke.
From 'afspreken' (to agree, arrange). Also means an agreement: 'afspraak is afspraak' = a deal is a deal. The Dutch plan social visits weeks ahead.

example.target: Ik heb morgen een afspraak bij de tandarts.
example.en: I have a dentist appointment tomorrow.

note: From Latin 'salarium', like 'salary'. 'Loon' is the more Germanic word for wages. 'Vakantiegeld' is the extra May holiday pay.
Borrowed from English with English pronunciation. Plural 'computers'. 'Laptop' is also used as is.
Strong verb: past 'schreef', participle 'geschreven'. From Latin 'scribere', like German 'schreiben'. 'Schrijver' = writer.

example.target: Ik schrijf een e-mail aan mijn baas.
example.en: I am writing an email to my boss.

note: Strong verb: past 'las' (plural 'lazen'), participle 'gelezen'. Note s/z: 'ik lees', 'wij lezen'. 'Lezer' = reader.

example.target: Hij leest elke avond een boek.
example.en: He reads a book every evening.

note: 'Wat is uw beroep?' = what do you do? From 'roepen' (to call), like English 'calling' or 'vocation'. 'Beroepsonderwijs' = vocational education.
Cognate with 'weather'. 'Weer' also means 'again' ('tot weer-ziens'). 'Mooi weer' = nice weather; 'weerbericht' = weather forecast.

example.target: Wat voor weer is het vandaag?
example.en: What is the weather like today?

note: Cognate with 'sun'. 'De zon schijnt' = the sun is shining. 'Zonnig' = sunny; 'zonnebril' = sunglasses; 'zondag' = Sunday.
Cognate with 'rain'. 'Regenjas' = raincoat; 'regenboog' = rainbow. The Dutch cycle through it rather than wait.
Used impersonally with 'het': 'het regent'. Regular past 'het regende', participle 'geregend'. 'Het regent pijpenstelen' = it is raining pipe stems (cats and dogs).

example.target: Het regent al de hele dag.
example.en: It has been raining all day.

note: Same spelling as English, pronounced 'vint'. 'Het waait' = it is windy. The flat land and sea make wind the defining Dutch weather feature.
Cognate with 'snow'; 'eeuw' is a long 'ay' followed by 'oo'. 'Het sneeuwt' = it is snowing. Rare enough in the Netherlands that it makes the news.
Related to the archaic English 'welkin' (sky). Plural 'wolken'. 'Bewolkt' = cloudy. The famous Dutch skies in paintings are full of them.
'On-' (un-, bad) + 'weer'. 'Het onweert' = there is a thunderstorm. 'Donder' = thunder, 'bliksem' = lightning.
Same as English. 'Het stormt' = it is stormy. 'Code oranje/rood' are the Dutch weather warnings. Plural 'stormen'.
Covers both warm and hot ('heet' is also used for very hot). 'Het is warm' = it is hot. 'Warme chocolademelk' = hot chocolate.
Cognate with 'cold'; 'ou' sounds like 'ow'. 'Ik heb het koud' (I have it cold) = I am cold. 'De kou' = the cold (noun).
Stress on the last syllable. Always in Celsius: 'twintig graden' = 20 degrees. 'Koorts' is a body temperature that is too high.
Used impersonally: 'het waait' = it is windy, 'het waait hard' = it is blowing hard. Past 'waaide' (older 'woei'), participle 'gewaaid'.

example.en: It is very windy at the seaside.

note: Plural 'bossen'. Also 'a bunch': 'een bos bloemen' = a bunch of flowers. The painter Hieronymus Bosch took his name from 's-Hertogenbosch.
Cognate with English 'beam' and German 'Baum'. Plural 'bomen'. 'Boompje' = sapling. 'Kerstboom' = Christmas tree.
Cognate with 'bloom'; also means 'flour'. Plural 'bloemen'. 'Bloemkool' (flower cabbage) = cauliflower. The Netherlands is the world's top flower exporter.

example.target: Ik koop bloemen op de markt.
example.en: I buy flowers at the market.

note: Came from the Ottoman Empire in the 1500s; the name goes back to Turkish 'tülbent' (turban). 'Tulpenmanie' in 1637 was the first famous speculative bubble.
Cognate with 'grass'. 'Grasveld' = lawn, field. 'Het gras maaien' = to mow the lawn.
Cognate with 'sea'. 'Noordzee' = North Sea; 'Zeeland' (sea land) is a province; New Zealand is named after it. 'Aan zee' = at the seaside.
Cognate with English 'strand' (shore). 'Naar het strand' = to the beach. Scheveningen and Zandvoort are the famous ones.
From French 'rivière'. Stress on '-vier'. The Rijn (Rhine), Maas and Waal are the big Dutch rivers. Plural 'rivieren'.
English 'dike/dyke' comes from this word. Thousands of kilometres of dykes keep the sea out; many surnames (Van Dijk, Dijkstra) come from it.
Land reclaimed from water and kept dry by dykes and pumps; borrowed into English as 'polder'. 'Poldermodel' = Dutch consensus politics.
Means both air and sky. 'Frisse lucht' = fresh air; 'blauwe lucht' = blue sky. 'Luchthaven' = airport. 'Ch' throat sound.
Cognate with 'cow'. Irregular plural 'koeien'. Black-and-white Holstein-Friesian cows come from the north of the Netherlands.
Originally 'corner' (compare German 'Winkel'), as shops were corners of a house. 'Winkelen' = to go shopping. 'Winkelcentrum' = shopping centre.
Albert Heijn ('de AH' or 'Appie'), Jumbo and Lidl are the big chains. Supermarkets are open late and on Sundays in most cities.
Cognate with 'market'. Most towns have a weekly 'markt' on the main square, often itself called 'de Markt'. 'Op de markt' = at the market.
Related to English 'yield' and 'gild'. 'Geld verdienen' = to earn money. 'Contant geld' = cash, increasingly rare in the Netherlands.

example.target: Ik heb geen geld bij me.
example.en: I have no money on me.

note: Stays singular after a number: 'tien euro'. The Netherlands and Belgium replaced the gulden and the Belgische frank in 2002.
Also singular after numbers: 'vijftig cent'. Dutch shops round cash totals to 5 cents; 1- and 2-cent coins are hardly used.
Cognate with 'price' and also means 'prize'. Plural 'prijzen'. 'Prijskaartje' = price tag.
Related to 'dear' in the old sense of costly. Inflected 'dure'. 'De duur' as a noun means duration. 'Te duur' = too expensive.
'Goed' + 'koop' (purchase). English 'cheap' developed the same way from 'good cheap' (a good bargain). Inflected 'goedkope'.
Irregular: past 'kocht', participle 'gekocht'. Cognate with 'cheap' and German 'kaufen'. 'Koopje' = a bargain.

example.target: Waar kan ik een kaartje kopen?
example.en: Where can I buy a ticket?

note: 'Ver-' + 'kopen'. Irregular like kopen: past 'verkocht', participle 'verkocht' (no ge- after ver-). 'Te koop' = for sale.
Regular: 'betaalde', 'betaald' (no ge- after be-). Related to 'tellen' (to count). 'Kan ik pinnen?' is how you ask to pay by card.
Usually third person: 'het kost', 'ze kosten'. Past 'kostte' (double t), participle 'gekost'. 'De kosten' = the costs.
'Hoeveel' (how much/many) is written as one word. Also 'Wat kost dit?'. Prices are shown including tax ('btw').
From Italian 'cassa'. Plural 'kassa's'. 'Zelfscankassa' = self-checkout. 'Kassabon' = receipt.
'Pin' from the PIN code, 'pas' = card. The Dutch pay almost everything by debit card; credit cards are far less accepted than in the US or UK.
A verb made from 'PIN'. Also to withdraw cash: 'geld pinnen' at a 'pinautomaat'. Regular: 'pinde', 'gepind'. Signs say 'alleen pinnen' (card only).

example.en: Can I pay by card here?

note: From 'korten' (to shorten, cut). 'Tien procent korting' = 10% off. 'Kortingscode' = discount code.
From French 'bon' (voucher). 'Kassabon' = till receipt; 'cadeaubon' = gift voucher. 'Wilt u de bon?' is asked at every till.
'Uit' + 'verkoop': selling out old stock. Signs say 'SALE' or 'uitverkoop'. 'Uitverkocht' = sold out.
From Latin 'gratis'. 'Free' as in freedom is 'vrij'. 'Gratis parkeren' = free parking. 'Voor niets' is the colloquial synonym.
Plural 'klanten'. 'De klant is koning' = the customer is king. 'Klantenservice' = customer service.
Past participle of 'sluiten' (to close). Shop signs: 'open' / 'gesloten'. Colloquially 'dicht' (shut) is used: 'de winkel is dicht'.
Cognate with 'baker'. 'Bij de bakker' = at the baker's. 'Bakkerij' is the shop; 'de bakker' is used for both.
From French 'porte-monnaie'. Stress on the last syllable; also spelled 'portemonnaie'. 'Geldbeugel' is the Flemish word.
Cognate with 'blithe'. 'Blij zijn met' = to be happy with. 'Blijdschap' = joy. Inflected 'blije'.

example.target: Ik ben blij dat je er bent.
example.en: I am glad you are here.

note: From 'verdriet' (sorrow, grief). 'Verdrietig zijn' = to be sad. 'Triest' and 'droevig' are near-synonyms.
'Boos zijn op iemand' = to be angry with someone. Also 'evil, wicked' in older or literary use ('de boze wolf'). 'Kwaad' is a synonym.

example.target: Waarom ben je boos op mij?
example.en: Why are you angry with me?

note: 'Bang zijn voor' = to be afraid of. 'Niet bang zijn!' = don't be scared. The noun is 'angst' or 'bangheid'.
One syllable, 'moo'. 'Doodmoe' (dead tired) = exhausted. 'Ik ben het zat' is 'I'm fed up', not 'moe'. Inflected 'moeie' or 'vermoeide'.

example.target: Ik ben moe, ik ga naar bed.
example.en: I am tired, I am going to bed.

note: From 'geluk', which means both happiness and luck, like German 'Glück'. As an adverb it means 'fortunately': 'gelukkig regent het niet'.
From French 'plaisir'. 'Veel plezier!' = have fun! 'Plezier hebben' = to enjoy yourself. Stress on the last syllable.
From 'voelen' (to feel). Plural 'gevoelens'. 'Op gevoel' = by feel. 'Gevoelig' = sensitive.
From 'lief' (sweet, dear), related to English 'love' and 'lief' (as in 'I'd as lief'). 'Liefje' = sweetheart. 'Liefs' ends informal letters.
'Ik hou van jou' = I love you (the d of 'houd' is usually dropped in speech and informal writing). Strong: past 'hield van', participle 'gehouden van'. Also for things: 'ik hou van kaas'.
Same word as German 'Angst', which English borrowed. 'Angst voor' = fear of. 'Angstig' = anxious. Plural 'angsten'.
From 'zenuw' (nerve) + '-achtig' (-like, -ish). 'Nerveus' is also used. 'Zenuwen hebben' = to have nerves (before an exam).

example.target: Ik ben zenuwachtig voor het examen.
example.en: I am nervous about the exam.

note: 'Verliefd zijn op' = to be in love with. From 'lief'. 'Verliefd, verloofd, getrouwd' = in love, engaged, married.
'Trots zijn op' = to be proud of. Also a noun: 'de trots' = pride. Related to German 'Trotz' (defiance).
From French 'jaloux'; the j is pronounced as in French ('zha-loers'). 'Jaloers op' = jealous of. 'Jaloezie' = jealousy, also a Venetian blind.
Participle of 'teleurstellen' (to disappoint), a separable verb: 'je stelt me teleur'. 'Teleurstelling' = disappointment.
Participle of 'verbazen' (to amaze). 'Verbaasd over' = surprised at. 'Verrast' is a pleasant surprise; 'verbaasd' is puzzled amazement.
Cognate with 'laugh'. Past 'lachte', but the participle is strong: 'gelachen'. 'Glimlachen' = to smile. 'Lachen om' = to laugh at.
Regular: 'huilde', 'gehuild'. 'Ui' sound. Related to 'howl'. Flemish often uses 'wenen' instead, which sounds old-fashioned in the Netherlands.
Regular: 'miste', 'gemist'. 'Ik mis je' = I miss you. Also to miss a train. 'Kwijt zijn' is used for losing things.
Borrowed from English. 'Stress hebben' = to be stressed. 'Gestrest' = stressed (adjective). Pronounced 'stres'.
From 'rust' (rest, peace). 'Rustig aan!' = take it easy. 'Een rustige straat' = a quiet street. 'Doe rustig' = calm down.
Reflexive: 'ik verveel me'. 'Vervelend' means annoying, not boring ('saai'). Regular: 'verveelde', 'verveeld'.
'Een' (one) + '-zaam', like German 'einsam'. 'Eenzaamheid' = loneliness. 'Alleen' just means alone, without the sadness.
From 'te vreden' (at peace, 'vrede' = peace). 'Tevreden met' = satisfied with. 'Ontevreden' = dissatisfied.

example.target: Ik ben tevreden met het resultaat.
example.en: I am satisfied with the result.

note: Strong: past 'zat' / 'zaten', participle 'gezeten'. Used far more than English 'sit': 'ik zit in de trein' = I'm on the train; 'hoe zit het?' = what's the situation?
Irregular: 'hij heeft', past 'had' / 'hadden', participle 'gehad'. Formal 'u heeft' or 'u hebt'. Cognate with 'have'.
Strong: past 'ging', participle 'gegaan'. Also forms the near future: 'ik ga eten' = I am going to eat. 'Hoe gaat het?' uses it.

example.en: We are going to the market.

note: Strong: past 'kwam' / 'kwamen', participle 'gekomen'. Note the short o in 'ik kom' but long in 'komen'. 'Kom binnen!' = come in.
Strong: past 'deed', participle 'gedaan'. 'Doe normaal' (act normal) is a very Dutch rebuke. Not used as a helper for questions: 'Werk je?' = do you work?
Regular: 'maakte', 'gemaakt'. Cognate with 'make'. 'Huiswerk maken', 'een foto maken' (take a photo), 'schoonmaken' (to clean).
Strong: past 'at' / 'aten', participle 'gegeten' (double ge-). Also the noun 'het eten' = food, the meal. 'Eet smakelijk!'
Strong, like English: 'dronk', 'gedronken'. 'Iets drinken' = to have a drink. 'Drinken' is also the noun for drink.

example.en: What would you like to drink?

note: Strong: past 'sliep', participle 'geslapen'. 'Slaap lekker!' = sleep well. 'Uitslapen' = to sleep in.
Separable: 'ik sta om zeven uur op'. Strong: past 'stond op', participle 'opgestaan'. Also 'to stand up' from a chair.

example.target: Ik sta elke dag om zeven uur op.
example.en: I get up at seven every day.

note: Strong: past 'zag' / 'zagen', participle 'gezien'. 'Tot ziens' = until seeing. 'Zie je?' = you see?
Regular: 'hoorde', 'gehoord'. Cognate with 'hear'. Also 'to belong': 'dat hoort zo' = that's how it should be.
Irregular past 'zei' / 'zeiden', participle 'gezegd'. 'Zeg!' is used to get attention ('hey!'). 'Hoe zeg je ... in het Nederlands?'
Strong: past 'sprak' / 'spraken', participle 'gesproken'. 'Praten' is the everyday 'to talk'. 'Spreekt u Engels?' = do you speak English?
Strong: past 'gaf' / 'gaven', participle 'gegeven'. 'Les geven' = to teach. 'Het geeft niet' = it doesn't matter.
Strong: past 'nam' / 'namen', participle 'genomen'. 'De trein nemen' = to take the train. 'Ik neem de soep' when ordering.

example.target: Ik neem de bus naar het werk.
example.en: I take the bus to work.

note: Modal verb: 'ik kan', 'jij kunt' (or 'kan'), past 'kon' / 'konden', participle 'gekund'. Followed by an infinitive at the end: 'ik kan goed zwemmen'.
Modal: 'ik wil', 'hij wil' (no -t), past 'wilde' or colloquial 'wou'. 'Ik wil graag' softens it to 'I would like'. Cognate with 'will'.
Modal: past 'moest', participle 'gemoeten'. 'Ik moet gaan' = I have to go. 'Moet dat?' = is that necessary? Cognate with 'must'.

example.en: I have to get up early tomorrow.

note: Irregular: past 'wist', participle 'geweten'. 'Ik weet het niet' = I don't know. Knowing a person or place is 'kennen'. Cognate with 'wit'.

example.target: Weet jij hoe laat het is?
example.en: Do you know what time it is?

note: Irregular: past 'dacht', participle 'gedacht', like English 'think / thought'. 'Denken aan' = to think of. 'Ik denk het' = I think so.
Regular: 'kookte', 'gekookt'. From Latin 'coquere', like 'cook'. Also 'to boil': 'het water kookt'. 'Kok' = a cook.
Strong: past 'keek', participle 'gekeken'. 'Tv kijken' = to watch TV; 'kijk uit!' = watch out. 'Even kijken' = let me see.
Strong: past 'vond', participle 'gevonden'. Also gives opinions: 'ik vind het lekker' = I think it's tasty. Note the spelling 'hij vindt' (d + t).

example.en: What do you think of Amsterdam?

note: Strong: past 'hielp', participle 'geholpen'. 'Kan ik u helpen?' is what shop staff say. 'Help!' is the same as English.
Cognate with 'what' (Dutch w = English wh). Also 'something/a bit': 'wat water' = some water; 'wat leuk!' = how nice!
Pronounced 'vee'. 'Wie is dat?' = who is that? 'Van wie' = whose. No separate 'whom'.
Cognate with 'where'. 'Waarheen' or 'waar ... naartoe' = where to; 'waarvandaan' = where from. Also means 'true' ('waar gebeurd' = really happened).
Question word for time. In statements 'als' (if/when, general) or 'toen' (when, past) is used instead: 'toen ik klein was'.
'Waar' + 'om' (about, for). The answer starts with 'omdat' (because). 'Daarom' = that's why.
Cognate with 'how', pronounced 'hoo'. 'Hoe gaat het?', 'hoe laat?', 'hoe lang?', 'hoeveel?' (how much/many).
'Welke' with de-words and plurals, 'welk' with het-words: 'welke fiets?', 'welk huis?'. Cognate with 'which'.
'Hoe' + 'veel' (much, many), one word. 'Hoeveel kost het?' = how much is it; 'de hoeveelste is het?' = what's the date?

example.en: How many children do you have?

note: Lowercase, unlike English 'I'. Cognate with 'I' (Old English 'ic'). Informal spoken form ''k'.
Stressed form; the unstressed 'je' is far more common ('heb je?'). 'Je' also means 'your'. Object form 'jou', possessive 'jouw'.
Polite form for strangers, officials and older people, with the 'he/she' verb form: 'u heeft' or 'u hebt'. Used more readily in Flanders than in the Netherlands.
Pronounced 'hay'. Unstressed 'ie' in speech ('heeft-ie?'). Object form 'hem', possessive 'zijn'. Dutch 'ij' here matches English 'he'.
Means both 'she' and 'they'; the verb tells you which ('zij is' / 'zij zijn'). Unstressed form 'ze' for both. Object: 'haar' (her), 'hen/ze' (them).
Stressed form; unstressed 'we' is usual. Object 'ons', possessive 'ons/onze'. Cognate with 'we'.
Cognate with 'and'. Pronounced 'en' with a short e. 'En jij?' = and you?
False friend: 'of' means 'or' (and 'whether'), not 'of'. English 'of' is 'van'. 'Koffie of thee?'

example.en: Do you want coffee or tea?

note: Also means 'only, just' ('maar één') and softens commands: 'kom maar' = just come, go ahead. Very frequent filler.
Negates verbs and adjectives; usually goes late in the sentence: 'ik kom niet'. Nouns with 'een' or no article are negated with 'geen' instead.
Replaces 'een' or no article to negate a noun: 'ik heb geen geld' (not 'niet geld'). Think 'I have no money'.
Pronounced 'oak'. Related to German 'auch'. 'Ik ook' = me too; 'ook niet' = neither.
Cognate with 'now'. Short 'nuu' with rounded lips. 'Nu' at the start of a sentence can also mean 'well, ...'. 'Tot nu toe' = until now.
Cognate with 'here', pronounced 'heer'. 'Hier is het' = here it is. Combines: 'hiervan' (of this), 'hierna' (after this).
Cognate with 'there'. 'Daarom' = therefore; 'daarna' = after that. 'Er' is the unstressed 'there' in 'er is / er zijn' (there is / are).
From 'het mag geschieden' (it may happen); pronounced 'mis-SCHEEN' with the throat sound. 'Eventueel' means 'possibly, if need be', not 'eventually'.
Sends the verb to the end: 'omdat ik moe ben'. 'Want' also means because but keeps normal word order: 'want ik ben moe'.

example.target: Ik blijf thuis omdat het regent.
example.en: I am staying home because it is raining.

note: Cognate with 'great'. Inflected 'grote' (one o before a vowel ending). 'Grootouders' = grandparents; 'groter' = bigger.
Same as German 'klein'; English 'clean' is the same word with a shifted meaning. 'Kleintje' = little one. Inflected 'kleine'.
Cognate with 'good'. Inflected 'goede' (often said 'goeie'). Comparative 'beter', superlative 'best', like English.
Related to German 'schlecht' and English 'slight'. 'Slecht weer' = bad weather. Comparative 'slechter', superlative 'slechtst'.
Used very broadly: 'mooi weer', 'mooie stad', 'mooi zo!' (well done). Pronounced 'moy'. Flemish often prefers 'schoon'.
'Het lelijke eendje' = the ugly duckling. Also used for 'nasty' ('een lelijke wond' = a nasty wound). 'Ij' sounds like 'ay'.
Cognate with 'new'. 'Nieuws' = the news; 'Nieuwjaar' = New Year. Inflected 'nieuwe'. New York was once Nieuw-Amsterdam.
Cognate with 'old'; 'ou' sounds like 'ow'. 'Hoe oud ben je?' = how old are you? Comparative 'ouder' also means 'parent'.
Cognate with 'young'. Inflected 'jonge'. 'Jongen' = boy; 'jongeren' = young people. 'Een jong' = a young animal.
Means both long and tall: 'hij is lang' = he is tall (the Dutch are the tallest people in the world). 'Hoe lang?' = how long/tall.
From Latin 'curtus', like 'curt'. 'Korting' (discount) comes from it. 'Kort geleden' = a short while ago.
Related to German 'schnell'. 'Snelweg' = motorway; 'sneltrein' = fast train. Also an adverb: 'snel!' = quick!
'Lang' + '-zaam', like German 'langsam'. Flemish usually says 'traag'. 'Langzaam maar zeker' = slowly but surely.
Colloquial form of 'gemakkelijk', from 'gemak' (ease, comfort). 'Makkie' = a piece of cake. Flemish often says 'gemakkelijk' in full.
From 'moeite' (effort, trouble). 'Moeilijk doen' = to be difficult (about something). 'Nederlands is niet zo moeilijk!'
The go-to word for anything pleasant: 'leuke film', 'leuke mensen', 'wat leuk!'. 'Eu' sound as in French 'deux'.
'Ik heb het druk' = I'm busy; 'het is druk' = it's crowded. Also 'pressure' and 'print' as a noun. 'Druk kind' = hyperactive child.
False friend: 'slim' means clever, not thin ('slank', 'dun'). English 'slim' was borrowed from Dutch, where it once meant 'crooked, sly'.
False friend: 'brutaal' is cheeky, bold or insolent, not brutal ('wreed'). 'Een brutaal kind' = a cheeky child.
False friend: 'eventueel' means 'possibly, should the need arise', never 'eventually' ('uiteindelijk'). 'Eventuele vragen' = any questions you may have.
Cognate with 'thick' (d for th). Means fat for people too. 'Dikke vrienden' = close friends; 'dik tevreden' = very satisfied.
Cognate with 'thin'. Inflected 'dunne'. For slim people 'slank' is the kinder word.
In the Netherlands 'schoon' means clean ('schoonmaken' = to clean). In Flanders it also means beautiful, its older sense. 'Schoonmoeder' = mother-in-law.
Cognate with 'full'. Inflected 'volle'. 'Vol is vol' on a sign = we are full. 'Volledig' = complete.
Inflected 'lege'. 'Leegstaan' = to stand empty (of buildings). 'Leeg' can also mean drained, exhausted.
Irregular plural 'steden'. 'Stadje' = small town. 'De stad in gaan' = to go into town. Cognate with 'stead' (as in 'homestead').

example.target: Utrecht is een mooie oude stad.
example.en: Utrecht is a beautiful old city.

note: Related to English 'thorp' in place names (Scunthorpe) and German 'Dorf'. Plural 'dorpen'. 'Dorpje' = little village.
From French 'plaine'. 'De Dam' in Amsterdam and 'het Plein' in The Hague are famous ones. 'Marktplein' = market square.
Cognate with 'church' and Scots 'kirk'. Many Dutch churches are now concert halls or bookshops. 'Kerkhof' = churchyard.
Plural 'musea' or 'museums'. The Rijksmuseum (national museum) in Amsterdam houses Rembrandt's 'Nachtwacht'. A 'museumkaart' gives a year's entry to hundreds.
Same as English. Plural 'parken'. The Vondelpark in Amsterdam is the best known. 'Parkeren' (to park a car) is a separate word.
From Greek via Latin, like French 'bibliothèque'. Stress on '-theek'. Shortened to 'de bieb' in speech. A 'boekhandel' is a bookshop.
'Stad' + 'huis'. Where you register when you move to the Netherlands ('inschrijven bij de gemeente'). Also 'gemeentehuis'.
Pronounced 'tay-AH-ter'. Flemish often uses 'schouwburg' (from 'schouwen', to view), which is also the name of many Dutch theatres.
From Greek 'bios' (life) + 'skopein' (to view), like the old English 'bioscope'. Shortened to 'de bios'. Films are subtitled, not dubbed.

example.target: Zullen we naar de bioscoop gaan?
example.en: Shall we go to the cinema?

note: 'Zwemmen' (to swim) + 'bad'. Dutch children get swimming diplomas (A, B, C) early, because of all the water.
'Dieren' (animals, cognate with 'deer') + 'tuin' (garden). Artis in Amsterdam (1838) is the oldest zoo in the Netherlands.
From Latin 'molina', like 'mill'. Mills drained the polders and ground grain. The 19 windmills at Kinderdijk are a UNESCO site. 'Molenaar' = miller.
From Latin 'castellum', like 'castle'. Plural 'kastelen'. Stress on '-teel'. Muiderslot near Amsterdam is a well-known one.
Cognate with 'haven'. Rotterdam has the largest port in Europe. 'Luchthaven' = airport (air harbour). Plural 'havens'.
Pronounced 'po-LEET-see'. 'Politiebureau' = police station. The emergency number is 112; 'politieagent' = police officer.
The local council you deal with for registration, permits and waste. From 'gemeen' (common, shared), like German 'Gemeinde'. Also a church congregation.
From 'buur' (neighbour). 'In de buurt' = nearby; 'in de buurt van' = near. 'Buurtwinkel' = corner shop.

example.target: Is er een supermarkt in de buurt?

note: From 'bouwen' (to build). Plural 'gebouwen'. 'Kantoorgebouw' = office building; 'hoofdgebouw' = main building.
From French 'fabrique'. Stress on '-briek'. Plural 'fabrieken'. 'Fabrikant' = manufacturer. A 'fabriek' is not a 'fabric' (stof).
Informal word for a pub or bar ('naar de kroeg gaan'). 'Oe' = 'oo'. 'Stamkroeg' = your regular pub; 'kroegentocht' = pub crawl.
'Brand' (fire, as in a blaze) + 'weer' (defence, as in 'afweer'). 'Brandweerman' = firefighter. Call 112.
A fitness centre is a 'sportschool' (sport school), not a 'gym'; 'gym' in Dutch means PE lessons at school. 'Fitness' is also used.
'Hoofd' (head, main) + 'stad'. Amsterdam is the capital, but the government and the king's office are in Den Haag (The Hague).
'Fietsen' + 'stalling' (from 'stal', stable). Utrecht station has the world's largest, with space for over 12,000 bikes.

example.target: De fietsenstalling is onder het station.
example.en: The bike parking is under the station.
